title: 2007 IMO Problem 4
statement:
In triangle \(ABC\) the bisector of \(\angle BCA\)
meets the circumcircle again at \(R\),
the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{BC}\) at \(P\),
and the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{AC}\) at \(Q\).
The midpoint of \(\overline{BC}\) is \(K\) and the midpoint of \(\overline{AC}\) is \(L\).
Prove that the triangles \(RPK\) and \(RQL\) have the same area.

solutions.text:
We first begin by proving the following claim.

Claim.
 We have \(CQ = PR\) (equivalently, \(CP = QR\)).

Proof.
 Let \(O = \overline{LQ} \cap \overline{KP}\) be the circumcenter.
 Then
 \[ \measuredangle OPQ = \measuredangle KPC = 90^\circ - \measuredangle PCK
 = 90^\circ - \measuredangle LCQ = \measuredangle \measuredangle CQL = \measuredangle PQO. \]
 Thus \(OP = OQ\).
 Since \(OC = OR\) as well, we get the conclusion.

Denote by \(X\) and \(Y\) the feet from \(R\) to \(\overline{CA}\)
and \(\overline{CB}\), so \(\triangle CXR \cong \triangle CYR\).
Then, let \(t = \frac{CQ}{CR} = 1 - \frac{CP}{CR}\).

[Diagram omitted from this imported TeX transcription.]

Then it follows that
\[ [RQL] = [XQL] = t(1-t) \cdot [XRC]
= t(1-t) \cdot [YCR] = [YKP] = [RKP] \]
as needed.

Remark.
 Trigonometric approaches are very possible
 (and easier to find) as well:
 both areas work out to be \(\frac 18 ab \tan \frac{1}{2} C\).
